The exact same barrier-based technique the original finding used (20 goroutines against one budget.Tracker/keyID, cap=$1, cost=$1 per request; every goroutine's OWN Reserve call completes before any goroutine's Reconcile call runs, via a sync.WaitGroup barrier honestly modeling the real upstream-call gap) now produces allowedCount=1/20 and finalSpent=$1.00 against cap=$1.00 -- reproducible across 5 consecutive runs (internal/budget/toctou_fix_test.go's TestConcurrentReserveReconcileBoundsAdmissionAgainstNearExhaustedCap and TestConcurrentReserveReconcileReproducibleAcrossManyRuns, both permanent, both passing under `go test -race`). The fix's own accepted trade-off (named, not hidden, in the RFC): a virtual key's very first-ever concurrent burst, before any real cost has been reconciled for it even once, is conservatively throttled to admit one request at a time (reserving the full remaining headroom, since no per-key cost history exists yet to calibrate a smaller reservation) -- self-resolving the moment any real cost is reconciled, never a permanent serialization of the key's traffic.

task_spec.research_ref: docs/upgrade-research/evals-corpus-cost-abuse-patterns-2026-09-08.md, Finding 5 / Concrete scenarios 3-4 (LiteLLM CVE-2026-47102 / GHSA-wpfp-gwwc-vwq6, CVE-2024-5710 / GHSA-qqcv-vg9f-5rr3) -- explicitly flagged by the research itself as privilege-escalation-in-kind rather than cost-abuse-in-kind, included here per this task's own category:routing carve-out for admin-API mutation surfaces
task_spec.description: CVE-2026-47102's root cause was a self-service endpoint whose ownership check was correct ('only your own account') but whose FIELD-level allowlist was missing, letting a caller mass-assign a privileged user_role field on their own record. CVE-2024-5710 let an authenticated caller manage teams other than their own because the access-control check was missing per-team scoping. Verified directly against admin.go: Handler (lines 83-89) wraps every route in requireBearerToken (lines 96-111), a single constant-time comparison against ONE static admin secret -- there is no identity.Verifier lookup anywhere in this package, no notion of 'this caller's own key' versus 'a different key', and upsertVirtualKeyHandler (lines 131-199) applies every POSTed field (KeyHash, BudgetUSD, AllowedModels, RateLimit incl. PerModel) to whatever virtual key `name` the caller specifies, by design -- a full, intentional replace, per the package's own doc comment describing this as 'a deliberately separate credential space' distinct from client-facing virtual keys.
task_spec.verified_against: gateway/internal/admin/admin.go:83-111 (Handler + requireBearerToken, single static-token check, no per-key ownership concept), :131-199 (upsertVirtualKeyHandler applies every field with no allowlist, by design), package doc comment lines 1-14
task_spec.corpus_note: Both LiteLLM CVEs require a narrowly-scoped/self-service caller whose access is supposed to be limited to 'their own' record or team -- that concept does not exist anywhere in Kelvran's Admin API v1: it is binary (the one static token grants full mutation rights over every virtual key, or no access at all). The specific 'ownership check correct, field allowlist missing' and 'no per-team scoping' bug SHAPES are therefore not currently reproducible against this surface, verified by direct code reading rather than assumed. This is a real, honestly-verified fact about today's code, not evidence of a hidden vulnerability -- but it is also a real regression guard for the future: if Kelvran ever adds a narrower-scoped or self-service key-mutation path (e.g. letting a caller rotate only their own key's metadata), that new path must enforce BOTH an ownership check AND a strict per-field allowlist from day one, per exactly the CVE-2026-47102 pattern -- a bare 'own record only' check would not be sufficient on its own, as that CVE itself demonstrates.

reference: Kelvran's Admin API v1 has exactly one credential tier (a single static bearer token) with no per-caller ownership/scope concept at all; every field of virtualKeyRequest is fully mutable by any holder of that token for any virtual key

task_spec.research_ref: docs/upgrade-research/evals-corpus-cost-abuse-patterns-2026-09-08.md, Finding 4 / Concrete scenario 5 (SkillBloat, arxiv.org/html/2608.21929v1) -- resolving that document's own Open Questions item 2
task_spec.description: SkillBloat demonstrates a malicious agent skill inflating a real multi-step coding-agent task's token consumption 26.39x (cost $0.21 -> $5.41) with every individual call unremarkable in isolation -- a stress test for whether a gateway's budget cap is checked before EVERY completion call in a long agentic run, or only once at session start. Verified directly: HandleChatCompletion (dataplane.go line 813) calls p.budget.Allow at line 870, and HandleChatCompletionStream (streaming.go line 61) calls the same p.budget.Allow at streaming.go line 109 -- both are the sole entry points for a completion call, both check unconditionally on every invocation, and neither reads from nor writes to any run-scoped cache of a prior Allow decision (no such cache exists anywhere in dataplane.Pipeline). A multi-step agentic run realized as N separate HTTP requests therefore re-checks Allow N times, never once for the whole run.
task_spec.corpus_note: This directly resolves the research's own stated open question favorably: Kelvran's per-request architecture (one HTTP request per completion call, no run/session object spanning several calls) means there is structurally no 'check once at run start' shortcut to exploit in the first place -- every individual completion call within a SkillBloat-style amplified run independently hits the real budget check. This does NOT mean a SkillBloat-style attack is fully mitigated: see the sibling case costabuse-no-cost-velocity-anomaly-signal for the real, honestly-named gap this same finding also surfaces (no anomaly signal below the flat cap), and see costabuse-budget-allow-record-toctou-race for how the per-call check itself is currently racy under concurrent load.

reference: budget.Tracker.Allow is called at the top of both HandleChatCompletion and HandleChatCompletionStream, with no run-level or session-level caching of the decision anywhere in the pipeline

task_spec.output: Kelvran enforces only a flat, binary total-spend cap (budget.Tracker.Allow) plus a log-only percent-of-cap warning (checkBudgetWarnThreshold); no cost-velocity, cost-per-minute, or cost-multiple-of-baseline anomaly signal exists anywhere in the codebase
task_spec.description: SkillBloat's whole point is that a 26x-75x cost blowup can happen with every individual call looking unremarkable -- invisible to any per-request check, and (per the sibling verified-safe case above) not hidden from the flat per-call budget cap either, but only visible in AGGREGATE, and only once the flat cap is actually hit or exceeded. Verified directly: grep across every .go file in internal/ for velocity/anomaly/baseline returns zero matches; the only spend-adjacent signal besides the hard cap itself is checkBudgetWarnThreshold (dataplane.go line ~1294), whose own doc comment states plainly it is 'log-only... never rejects or alters the request' and re-logs on every billable completion while spend remains over a single static percent-of-cap threshold -- not a rate/velocity/baseline-relative measure of any kind.
task_spec.verified_against: repo-wide grep for velocity/anomaly/baseline across gateway/internal/ (zero matches); gateway/internal/gateway/dataplane/dataplane.go:1294 (checkBudgetWarnThreshold doc comment, log-only flat-percent-of-cap warning)
task_spec.corpus_note: A real, currently-not-built gap, honestly named rather than fixed here (out of this task's scope) -- output and reference deliberately differ, the same documented-gap convention this corpus already established for the guardrail Phase 2 cases (e.g. regcorpus-guardrail-13). Under today's real per-key budget_usd caps (commonly generously sized for legitimate agentic workloads), a SkillBloat-style amplification could run for a long time inside the flat cap's headroom, with zero signal distinguishing it from ordinary heavy-but-legitimate usage until the cap itself is finally hit -- a real, named backlog candidate (per_agent_run_id cost-per-minute, or cost-vs-that-task-shape's-own-historical-baseline), not evidence of a coding bug in existing logic.

task_spec.description: Scenario 14 asks whether a cache hit's cost is ever computed from a stale or estimated token count rather than being cleanly excluded from provider-usage-based billing. task_spec.description: Scenario 2 asks whether a leaked/stolen provider API key's blast radius is bounded by the compromised virtual key's own budget_usd cap rather than by the shared provider credential's full available spend. Verified directly by reading gateway/internal/gateway/dataplane/dataplane.go's Deployment struct (lines 107-113: Name/Model/Provider/UpstreamModel/BaseURL/APIKey, plus AccessKeyID/SecretAccessKey/SessionToken for bedrock) and gateway/internal/budget/budget.go's Tracker.Allow signature (line 139: keyID string, capUSD decimal.Decimal, resetInterval time.Duration -- no Deployment/credential parameter at all). A Deployment is resolved via p.nextDeployment(req.Model) -> p.router.Select(model) -> p.deploymentsByName[name] (dataplane.go lines 1068-1075), a lookup keyed entirely on the canonical model name, never on vk.ID or any credential value. Budget enforcement (dataplane.go:870, streaming.go:109) is therefore structurally scoped to the caller's own virtual key regardless of which Deployment/APIKey/AWS-credential-set ends up serving the request -- the same provider credential can back many deployments used by many different virtual keys, but each virtual key's own Allow/Record accounting is independent and unaffected by which credential is riding along underneath a given call.

task_spec.corpus_note: REAL, VERIFIED GAP -- not fixed in this pass (corpus authoring only), and narrower than the already-converted costabuse-budget-allow-record-toctou-race case: that case is about TWO SEPARATE requests racing each other's Allow/Record calls; this case is about ONE already-approved request's own single stream having no re-check mechanism at all once it starts, regardless of any race. In practice a long streamed completion (many output tokens, real generation time) is exactly the shape of request most likely to still be in flight when a sibling request's Record call pushes the key over its cap -- the already-running stream is never interrupted by that. Not claimed to be exploitable with high severity on its own (the stream was legitimately approved at the moment it started), but a real, honest gap relative to the research scenario's own framing of 'rejected even mid-stream.'

reference: an already-approved streaming response should be interrupted mid-stream once the caller's own budget cap is crossed (e.g. by another concurrent request on the same vk.ID recording spend while this stream is still being written), not allowed to run to completion unconditionally once the single upfront check passes

task_spec.description: fallback_chains (shipped, docs/rfcs/2026-09-07-gateway-error-classified-fallback-chains.md) explicitly, deliberately, and by design permits a fallback hop to a deployment serving a DIFFERENT model than the one the client requested -- config.example.yaml's own comment names the canonical example directly ('a context-window-exceeded error warrants a larger-context model... claude-opus-4 has a bigger context window than gpt-4o'). Verified directly: dataplane.go:1247's finalize computes cost via `p.costCalc.Calculate(req.Model, ...)` -- req.Model is the CLIENT'S ORIGINALLY-REQUESTED model string, never dep.Model (the deployment that actually served the response) or resp.Model (which callDeployment, dataplane.go:1083, deliberately overwrites BACK to req.Model too, 'matching the convention of OpenAI-shaped APIs'). When a fallback_chains hop swaps to a genuinely different, more expensive model, the ENTIRE cost calculation -- and therefore budget.Tracker.Reconcile's real dollar debit against the virtual key's cap -- is priced using the ORIGINALLY-REQUESTED (cheap) model's price-table entry, not the model that actually generated the tokens and incurred the real upstream cost.

task_spec.description: checkRateLimit(ctx, vk, req.Model) (dataplane.go:869) runs BEFORE routing/fallback resolution, keyed exclusively on req.Model -- the client's originally-requested model, per docs/rfcs/2026-09-07-gateway-multi-dimensional-rate-limits.md's own PerModel design ('checked before falling back to this key's own default bucket'). There is no equivalent re-check anywhere after a fallback_chains hop switches to a different actual model. An operator who configures a strict PerModel RPM cap specifically to bound load/spend on an EXPENSIVE model (e.g. gpt-4o) while leaving a cheap model (gpt-4o-mini) generously capped has that gpt-4o cap entirely unenforced for any traffic that reaches gpt-4o via a gpt-4o-mini request's own fallback_chains hop -- the exact same real, documented, shipped feature the sibling billing case exploits.

task_spec.corpus_note: Genuinely new, previously-undocumented -- not fixed in this pass, out of scope per this task's own instructions. A real security/cost-governance bypass, not just a cost-math discrepancy: an adversarial or merely opportunistic caller can deliberately trigger the fallback path (e.g. by sending a prompt sized just past the cheap model's own context window) to reach an otherwise rate-capped expensive model at will, with the operator's own PerModel cap providing zero protection for that specific access path.

reference: a virtual key's PerModel rate-limit override for a given model should be enforced for every request that ends up actually served by that model, including one reached via a fallback_chains hop from a different originally-requested model -- not only for requests that name that model directly

task_spec.research_ref: Direct code-reading + live verification exercise against gateway/internal/budget's Reserve/reservationAmountLocked during this corpus-authoring pass, following up on docs/rfcs/2026-09-08-gateway-budget-ratelimit-toctou-fix.md's own already-named-and-accepted 'cold-start conservatism' trade-off -- this case verifies that trade-off's exact, extreme real magnitude precisely rather than only its qualitative description, and confirms it is NOT a new gap.
task_spec.description: budget.Tracker.reservationAmountLocked reserves a key's own historical average real cost once billing history exists (billedCount > 0), or -- on a cold start, billedCount == 0 -- the FULL remaining headroom under the cap. docs/rfcs/2026-09-08-gateway-budget-ratelimit-toctou-fix.md's own 'Alternatives Considered' section explicitly rejected a smaller, proportional cold-start reservation specifically because it 'fails to bound admission to the required "at most one"' for exactly this shape -- meaning the documented, INTENDED design is that a brand-new key's very first concurrent burst admits at most one request until real cost is reconciled. This case verifies that intended behavior's exact real magnitude is as extreme as the RFC's own reasoning implies: the first Reserve call on a cold key consumes 100% of the configured cap as its provisional reservation, not merely 'a large chunk' -- so ANY concurrent sibling call before that first call reconciles is unconditionally rejected, regardless of how small its real eventual cost would be.
task_spec.verified_against: gateway/internal/budget/budget.go:297-302 (reservationAmountLocked: billedCount==0 returns capUSD.Sub(spent[keyID]), the full remaining headroom); budget.go:265-281 (Reserve). A temporary Go probe test in internal/budget, run and deleted before this pass's own final commit: two sequential Reserve calls against the same brand-new key with a $100 cap -- call 1 returns (allowed=true, reserved=true, reservedUSD="100"); call 2, before call 1's Reconcile, returns (allowed=false, reserved=false, reservedUSD="0"); Reconcile(call1) with a real cost of $0.01 leaves SpentUSD="0.01" -- confirming the reservation was exactly the full cap, not a partial/proportional amount, and that it correctly unwinds to the real, tiny cost once reconciled.
task_spec.corpus_note: This is NOT a newly-found bug -- docs/rfcs/2026-09-08-gateway-budget-ratelimit-toctou-fix.md already names and explicitly accepts this exact trade-off by design ('reserve everything, admit one' is the RFC's own phrase), and its Alternatives Considered section already rejected the one candidate fix (proportional reservation) that would have softened it. Encoded here as a PASS case, matching this corpus's established practice of verifying an already-documented, accepted limitation's precise real behavior against the live code (e.g. the guardrail corpus's case 13, adversarial-cache-static-key-decorator-not-applicable) -- not as a FAIL/gap case, since the behavior matches the documented design intent exactly.

reference: Reserve(fresh_key, cap=$100)_call_1=allowed_true_reservedUSD_$100 (100% of the cap, on a brand-new key with zero billing history); Reserve(fresh_key, cap=$100)_call_2_before_call_1_reconciles=allowed_false_reservedUSD_$0; after call_1 reconciles with its real cost of $0.01, spent=$0.01

task_spec.research_ref: Direct code-reading + live verification exercise against gateway/internal/ratelimit's TokenBucket.ReserveTPM/reservationAmountLocked during this corpus-authoring pass, confirming whether the sibling budget.Tracker.Reserve cold-start-conservatism finding (costabuse-budget-reserve-coldstart-conservatism-verified-exact-magnitude) transfers identically to the TPM dimension -- verified independently rather than assumed to transfer, per this task's own explicit instruction.
task_spec.description: ratelimit.TokenBucket.reservationAmountLocked mirrors budget.Tracker's identical cold-start design: billedCount==0 reserves the bucket's full current balance (b.tokens), not a historical average. An initial assumption that this would behave byte-identically to the budget.Tracker case (a second concurrent call always rejected outright) turned out to be WRONG when first tested against a real, non-frozen clock -- TokenBucket continuously refills based on real elapsed time (refillLocked, called at the top of every ReserveTPM), so even a few microseconds between two sequential Go statements adds back a small amount of balance, letting a second call succeed with a tiny, non-deterministic reservation. Re-verified with a frozen clock (NewTokenBucketWithClock, zero elapsed time) to isolate the TRUE zero-time-elapsed case: under that condition, the behavior is exactly identical to budget.Tracker's -- the second call is flatly rejected. In real production traffic (a real, non-frozen clock, nonzero true elapsed time between concurrent requests), TPM's continuous refill provides a small, real-time-dependent mitigating cushion that budget.Tracker's non-refilling cumulative USD cap structurally cannot have at all -- a genuine, verified DIFFERENCE between the two subsystems' cold-start behavior in practice, not merely a restatement of the same finding twice.
task_spec.verified_against: gateway/internal/ratelimit/ratelimit.go:147-154 (reservationAmountLocked: billedCount==0 returns b.tokens, clamped to zero); ratelimit.go:125-134 (ReserveTPM, calls refillLocked() before checking/reserving). A temporary Go probe test in internal/ratelimit, run and deleted before this pass's own final commit, run twice: once against NewTokenBucket (a real, non-frozen clock) -- call 1 reserved 100000 (the full capacity), call 2 UNEXPECTEDLY succeeded with reservedTokens=1.459792 (a small, real-elapsed-time-dependent refill); once against NewTokenBucketWithClock with a frozen fakeClock (matching this codebase's own existing determinism-testing convention in ratelimit_test.go) -- call 1 reserved 100000, call 2 correctly returned allowed=false, reservedTokens=0, matching budget.Tracker's own behavior exactly under the true zero-elapsed-time condition.
task_spec.corpus_note: Like the sibling budget case, this is NOT a newly-found bug -- the same docs/rfcs/2026-09-08-gateway-budget-ratelimit-toctou-fix.md RFC explicitly covers 'gateway/internal/ratelimit's TPM equivalents' using the identical reservation-sizing design and Alternatives-Considered reasoning. Encoded as a PASS case. The one genuinely new, worth-recording nuance this verification pass adds beyond the RFC's own text: the two subsystems' cold-start behavior is NOT byte-identical in real production conditions, only under an idealized zero-elapsed-time model -- a distinction the RFC's own prose does not call out, discovered here specifically because this task's own discipline required independently re-verifying the transfer rather than assuming it, and the FIRST (non-frozen-clock) probe run genuinely surprised the outcome expected from the budget sibling before the frozen-clock rerun clarified why.
